pass_a_gloss: And of what sort martyrdom is, and how much free speech it works in toward God, it is possible to learn thoroughly from here too. The holy man, being someone ambitious for honour and wanting to repay the good deeds that have reached him beforehand from God, seeks what he might do to the Lord concerning all things which he has taken from him; and he finds nothing else, as if equal in weight to the good deeds, able to be given back to God by a man of good choice, as the end in martyrdom. For it is written in the hundred and fifteenth psalm, the things of the perplexity thus: what shall I give back in return to the Lord concerning all that he gave back to me; and the things of the meeting reply to it, someone having said: what will the one saying this give back to the Lord concerning all he has taken from him, said thus: a cup of salvation I shall take and the name of the Lord I shall call upon. And it is a custom for martyrdom to be named cup of salvation, as we found in the gospel. For when those wanting to be seated with Jesus out of right and out of left in his kingdom reach out for greater honour, the Lord says to them: are you able to drink the cup which I drink, saying cup for martyrdom. Which is plain also from: Father, if possible, carry this cup aside from me; except not what I want but what you. Except we learn that the one having drunk that cup, which Jesus drank, will sit together and reign together and judge together with the king of those reigning. This then is the cup of salvation, which the one taking will call on the name of the Lord; and all who might call on the name of the Lord will be saved.
pass_b_english: What martyrdom is, and how much boldness toward God it brings about, can be learned from this too. The saint, being generous of spirit and wishing to repay the benefits that have come to him from God, asks what he might do for the Lord in return for all that he has received from him; and he finds nothing else that a person of good will could give back to God which would, as it were, balance those benefits, as death in martyrdom does.

For in the hundred and fifteenth Psalm (by the Greek count) the words of the perplexed question are written thus: “What shall I give back to the Lord for all that he has given me?” (Psalm 116:12). And when it has been asked, “What will the one who says this give back to the Lord for all that he has received from him?”, the words of the answer are these: “I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord” (Psalm 116:13).

It is customary to call martyrdom the cup of salvation, as we have found in the Gospel. For when those who wished to sit at the right and at the left of Jesus in his kingdom were reaching for a greater honour, the Lord says to them, “Can you drink the cup that I drink?” (Matthew 20:22), calling martyrdom a cup. This is clear also from the words, “Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me; yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36; Matthew 26:39). But we learn that the one who drinks that cup which Jesus drank will sit with, reign with and judge with the King of those who reign. This, then, is the cup of salvation: whoever takes it will call on the name of the Lord, and “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 28); the old English was misaligned: it ran on into the matter of chapters 29 and 30 (Psalm 116:15, the baptism of martyrdom, the heavenly altar, blemished priests) and dropped this chapter's own argument: the saint's search for a return to God, the question-and-answer reading of Psalm 116:12-13, the request of the sons of Zebedee, and the promise that whoever drinks the cup reigns and judges with the King.
